title: Valley of Flowers & Hemkund Sahib
summary: A striking dual alpine landscape: an emerald valley carpeted in hundreds of monsoon wildflower species, paired with a steep, punishing ascent to a sacred high-altitude glacial lake wrapped in mist.
story: Stepping into the Valley of Flowers feels like crossing the threshold into a living canvas. Hemmed in by massive, misty mountain walls, the valley floor transforms completely under monsoon showers, shifting its color palette weekly as rare endemic blooms compete for space.

The next dawn completely changes the tone. The trek up to Hemkund Sahib is a relentless, gravity-defying climb. Pushing through thin air at 4,632 meters, the rewards hit all at once: a completely silent crystal tarn, floating ice sheets, and the quiet devotion echoing from the world's highest Gurudwara.

title: Kedarkantha
summary: A winter classic. Snow-loaded pines, a frozen summit climb at dawn, and a 360-degree ring of Himalayan peaks at the top.
story: Kedarkantha is the trek that hooks people on winter mountaineering. Snow from the first day, a magical campsite in the pines, and a summit dawn with peaks in every direction.
Simple, accessible, and unforgettable - the perfect introduction to snow.

title: Badrinath & Vasudhara Falls
summary: A Char Dham pilgrimage that extends beyond the temple — past India's last village at the Tibetan border, and up a rocky high-altitude trail to a sacred 400-foot waterfall said to touch only the pure of heart.
story: Badrinath at 3,300 meters is already a world apart — flanked by the Nar and Narayana ranges, the Alaknanda rushing below, Nilkantha towering above. But the journey doesn't end at the temple gates. Mana Village, a short drive away and the last settlement before Tibet, opens the door to the real high country.

From Mana, a 6 km trek on rocky terrain climbs to Vasudhara Falls at 3,658 meters. The waterfall drops 400 feet off a sheer cliff face, and the legend holds that its spray only touches those who are pure of heart. Standing there with Chaukhamba, Nilkantha, and Balakun filling the skyline, it's easy to believe it.

title: Chandrashila & Tungnath
summary: A summit that earns its reputation — Chandrashila's 4,000-meter peak delivers one of the most complete Himalayan panoramas in Garhwal, with Nanda Devi, Trishul, Chaukhamba, and Bandarpunch all in a single unbroken sweep.
story: The route up from Chopta passes through Tungnath Temple — the world's highest Shiva temple at 3,680 meters — but Chandrashila summit at 4,000 meters is the real destination. The final stretch breaks free of the treeline completely, leaving nothing between you and a full 360-degree ring of snow peaks.

On a clear day the view is almost disorienting in its scale. Peaks you've only seen individually suddenly appear together — Nanda Devi, Trishul, Chaukhamba, Kedar Dome, Bandarpunch — lined up across the horizon in every direction.

title: Aadi Kailash & Om Parvat
summary: The high, remote corner of Kumaon near the Tibet border — Aadi Kailash above the sacred lakes of Gauri Kund and Parvati Kund at around 5,400 m, and the snow-written ॐ on Om Parvat.
story: This is the far end of the map. The road clings to sheer cliffs above the Kali river, villages thin out after Gunji, and an inner-line permit is the only way in. Every hour the air gets thinner and the silence gets bigger.

Then the valley opens: Aadi Kailash rising white above Parvati Kund, the still blue water of Gauri Kund at its feet, prayer flags snapping in the wind at the Om Parvat viewpoint, and the snow on its face tracing the sacred syllable exactly as people describe it. Standing up there at around 5,400 m, breathing hard and grinning harder, is the place I think about most when I need to remember why the hard parts are worth it.

title: Gangotri, Gaumukh–Tapovan & Yamunotri
summary: To the sources of the Ganga and the Yamuna — a trail of temples, granite gorges and glacial rivers to Gaumukh, the snout of the Gangotri glacier, and on up to the Tapovan meadow at 4,200 m.
story: Two rivers, two journeys. The Yamunotri climb is short and steep, shared with pilgrims and ponies all the way to the temple. Gangotri is different — a town of bells and cold mist, with the Bhagirathi thundering through a granite gorge below.

Beyond Gangotri the trail leaves the crowds behind. Deodar gives way to bare moraine, the Bhagirathi peaks fill the horizon, and at Gaumukh the river is born straight out of the ice. Above it, a scramble across the glacier leads to Tapovan at 4,200 m, with Shivling standing right over the meadow. I timed the return with the closing ceremony, when the goddess's doli is carried down for winter — music, marigolds and an entire valley turning out to say goodbye.

title: Kashmir — Four Years in the Valley
summary: Four years at NIT Srinagar turned Kashmir into my backyard — Dal Lake mornings, Gulmarg snow, Sonamarg glaciers, Pahalgam meadows and the climb to Tulian Lake.
story: I went to Srinagar for an engineering degree and came back with a second education in mountains. Weekends meant chasing a different valley: shikaras on Dal Lake, autumn chinars turning the campus red, the first snowfall that made everyone forget exams for a day.

Gulmarg taught me to ski badly and laugh about it. Sonamarg showed me my first glacier up close. Pahalgam's meadows became the default answer to 'where this weekend?', and the long walk up to Tulian Lake, at 3,684 m, was the first time altitude really got under my skin. A lot of what I am started here.

title: Kedarnath
summary: A 16 km climb along the Mandakini to one of the oldest Shiva temples in the Himalaya, set against a wall of snow peaks at 3,583 m.
story: The walk up from Gaurikund follows the Mandakini the whole way — waterfalls spilling onto the trail, pilgrims of every age moving at their own pace, and the valley narrowing until the snow peaks close it off ahead.

Then the temple appears: dark stone, marigold garlands and the Kedarnath range glowing behind it. I've been back more than once, and the moment never gets old — the evening aarti, the town lit up under the stars, and dawn painting the peaks gold above a sea of tents.

title: My Village
summary: Terraced fields, slate-roofed houses, monsoon mist and winter snow on Anchriyanda Top above — the village where every trek of mine really began.
story: Before I knew the word 'trek', I knew these hills. Terraced fields stepping down to the river, a small temple at the centre of the village, cattle that know the way home better than any map, and Anchriyanda Top rising to 2,900 m above it all, turning white every winter.

I come back whenever I can — to walk the old paths in the monsoon mist, climb the same trees I climbed as a kid, plough a field for an afternoon, and sit on Anchriyanda Top in the snow with friends. Every summit since has, in some way, been an attempt to find this feeling somewhere higher.

title: Nag Tibba
summary: The 'Serpent's Peak' — a short, beautiful weekend trek through oak forest to a summit with the Bandarpunch and Gangotri ranges laid out in front of you.
story: Nag Tibba is the trek I keep recommending to friends: close enough for a weekend, high enough to feel like the real thing. I've done it twice — once in the green of July, camping in the mist with a tricolour flying over the tent, and once in February, breaking trail through knee-deep snow.

The reward is the summit morning. The sun comes up over ridge after ridge, and the whole Garhwal Himalaya — Bandarpunch, Swargarohini, the Gangotri group — lines up across the horizon. A camp dog adopted us both times.

title: Surkanda Devi & Tehri
summary: An Independence Day ride to Tehri lake and the Dobra-Chanti bridge, then a short, steep climb to Surkanda Devi temple floating above a sea of clouds.
story: A long weekend and a tricolour in the backpack. We rode out on Independence Day along the shores of Tehri lake, crossed the Dobra-Chanti suspension bridge high above the water and stopped at the jetty to watch the boats drift across the reservoir.

The next morning was the short, steep climb to Surkanda Devi. Near the top the clouds dropped below us, and the temple stood bright against a clean blue sky — a small trek with one of the biggest views in Garhwal.
